Post-Lockdown Food Gardens

By: Liz Fish | Delivery

Proposal


Show:

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Cape Town Together Food Growers turning the crisis of COVID 19 into long term survival

Unique Selling Point:
Some incredible things have come out of COVID 19 and one of them is a network of Urban Food Growers that has taken off across Cape Town and is now spreading to the Garden Route and KZN. The desperation for food combined with the weirdness of being stuck in isolation with the only outreach being through zoom broke down barriers created by access to money and resources and instead people reached out all connected via technology- the instigator of the group Eric Inches has never been seen on zoom and has co-ordinated this from her bedroom at the foot of Sir Lowry Pass

Summary:
Urban food gardens have existed in Cape Town for years, but they tend to be isolated little pockets in back yards and school grounds, what COVID 19 did was link people across the City in networks that never existed before. People stopped competing and started talking and supporting each other. The food crisis was so extreme that people from wealthy suburbs linked up with poorer suburbs and formed CAN groups- Citizen Action Groups. But this was far more than soup kitchens and food aid, this is long term shift in thinking. People started to help each other with bakkie loads of manure, seeds, composting and which revitalised abandoned or struggling gardens. Urban farmers started connecting across the City doing it for themselves and putting food into the soup kitchens and into their communities.


Further information:
What was fascinating is that data bundles and whatsapp bundles provided by the City gave people a chance to reach join and form the Food Growers Network where they could access support and give support. Erica Inches stuck in room at the foot of Sir Lowry pass just outside Somerset West in lockdown, started linking people. With a background in permaculture, a life coach and system analyst she has an interesting set of skills. The Cape Town Together - CTT Food growers initiative has no leaders and no rules, just kindness and support, and in the last 5 months there has been a radicle transformation amongst urban food growers. The vegetables they grow are not leaving for the leafy suburbs through NGO’s they are being eaten in the communities in which they grown. These urban farmers are accessing knowledge and support from each other on how to cultivate the harsh sandy soils of the Cape Flats and produce organic vegetables. Being a farmer is hard, dirty work and dismissed as inferior work by the youth but COVID has shifted that, young people have got involved and begun to work alongside the women and old people.
Zoom workshops on how to compost, donations of seeds, sharing worm farms, and support to transform barren, unarable strips of land littered with glass and concrete through ingenious methods has been inspiring.

Script:


Link: Urban food gardens like this are thriving across Cape Town - Lockdown plunged so many communities into a food crisis and soup kitchens sprung up everywhere. But what’s emerged 9 months later are these incredible networks of urban farmers
Script: Its market day for Oceanview organic farm. Run by 5 women who call themselves the Kos Gangsters, they struggling to keep up with the demands of preparing 80 boxes of veggies for sale this morning into into the local communities and baking bread for the soup kitchens. Sophia Grodes is the driving force
Sophia “When we came here, we knew nothing. We came from retail workers, housewives, teachers. We had our own careers. We knew nothing about farming. We were caterpillars. ….and we turned into butterflies. I don't want to be a caterpillar ever again

Script: And that pretty much sums up what many urban farmers feel about the connections established this year. Across Cape Town there are 160 different Community Action Networks, known as CANS. They are groups of people that came together in the beginning of lockdown to provide support for the neighbours, resourced communities partnered with under resourced communities. Initially to provide food relief but these relationships transformed into ongoing partnerships.

Erica: We were all talking about food aid and we're all talking about how are we going to make this last? And we know that we're going to run out of everybody else's money. ….And the best way is by growing our food.

Script: Erica Inches started The Cape Town Together Food Growers initiative and there are now 11 different Whataspp groups, and facebook page trading seeds, running education workshops, and exchanging resources

Erica: I used my fortune that I've had in life to try and help other people, because really anybody that's my age in South Africa, that this time should be paying back into the country.

Script: Stuck in lockdown with a background in finance management and permaculture, she says she is just joining the dots between the growers, NGOs, and the specialists. But that's taken 18 hours a day for the last 9 months, and to date no one has ever seen her face

Masa: It seems what this initiative has done is also connect really small farmers into this big network.

Erica: Yes, all of these voices that were unheard before are being heard ….

Script: Vuyani Qamata has been struggling to make a go of it in the school gardens for years, and when COVID hit he found himself locked out of the school and worried how he would feed his family. He joined the Gugulethu CAN and suddenly he was connected into the resources of the Seapoint CAN. There are many urban farmers dotted around Gugs and this was the chance for them to get organised. So far they’ve built 13 new gardens and formed the Gugulethu Urban Farmers Initiative GUFI

Vuyani: you had the support of people opening their hearts, opening their hands, you know, from more priviledged areas. And it's unbelievable that kind of support and what it did for us.

Link: This is what this space looked like before lockdown, fast forward 9 months later and its been transformed into this incredible food garden
Script: Busi Selana was sick with anxiety at the start of lockdown, her husband and brother both lost their jobs and she feared how long hers would last. Her son suggested they try and grow some veggies to feed the family of 6

Masa: Busi what an impressive garden you have here. Now, I'm told before lockdown, this was not the case here.

Busi: Definitely not.
Masa “What was here,
Busi “ooh is just plain sand, plain sand.

Busi One day my tap over there was leaking. I called my neighbour to come along to just check it out. And fortunately for me, he's like, what are you guys starting here, is it like a garden. That is like, nope, hell no, not like this. I'll show you how I'll bring a team three daysThis is what came about.

Script: Now she is a convert, before lockdown she had no interest in gardens

Busi “It brought a lot of joy, because now I don't necessarily have to go to the stores to go and buy..

Script: Vuyani happens to be her neighbour who had created his secret garden just over her back wall and she had no idea it existed, apart from the sounds of his chickens

Vuyani: even more amazing was that we even managed to attract a part of our society, which had no interest at all in farming or gardening and that was the youth.

Link: This is the beginning of a dream of the Gugulethu urban food garden initiative where they aim to turn Gugs into a food forest and also to have people wake up to the sound of birds chirping
Script: These gardens are havens of hope, in Mfuleni Hazel Nyaba garden is full of hearts which says it all

Hazel: whenever I'm sad I don't have another place to go whenever I want my me time. I don't have another place to go. I have to come here and meditate.

Script: Starting out in a small garden alongside her house she is clinging onto a patch across the road that she is defending from the encroaching shacks

Masa: how is CTT food growers benefiting you

Hazel: “ The information that they are sending, it's helping, the solution that you give another farmer I also get that solution so that I can use it in my garden.

Masa: I also hear there is also an exchanging of seeds and plants.

Hazel: Ja, I have to save seeds so that I can also give back

Script: That’s exactly how Nomalanga Ruiters managed to get herself started, it was on seed donations through the whatsapp group. In June this was a barren sandy patch, Nomalanga and her husband Sipho have turned it into a beacon of hope for those around her
Nomulanga: Covid-19 impacted my life in such a drastic where by one minute I had a place to stay, the next minute I was evicted because of not being able to pay rent. ….I used to go to soup kitchens. Then I realized that I spent half of my day waiting for a plate of food that I don't know when it's going to come. And I decided, you know what, I can always collect compost and put it into the ground and try and start up a small garden

Script: The more she started posting about her garden the more people supported her

Nomulanga: the minute we started that network, that's whereby we realized that so many of us in the location and most of us are doing great work, but we don't really get that connection or recognition.

Script: We visited her a month after she started this school garden

Nomulunga: when they approached me, I was already rejected by four schools around the location when I went to ask for grounds in order to start a food garden. But the aim of accepting the offer was because I wanted to incorporate what I do into the school curriculum.

Script: bEveryone we spoke to told us of their struggle to access large enough pieces of land to make farming viable. The City won’t give access even to dumping sites, and people are building on every little corner. Water and markets are the other thing holding them back

Vuyani: the frustration in dealing with government the bureaucracy you know, these things that we're getting now, we applied for them in 2017. And at's one of the things that has made it necessary, that there is a forum to really engage government

Erica: our backyard gardeners that have come onto the network and are starting to show results of what they doing the Department of Agriculture is meeting up with them through the network and started to help them.

Script: Every week via zoom they sharing their problems and knowledge from seed - to water harvesting and how they going to tackle bureaucracy

Script:COVID kick started the connection but they’re now solid partnerships. Clovelly and Kommetjie CAN donated the oven and all the equipment for the Kos Gangsters restaurant and continue to raise funds for the bread and soup mix supplied to many soup kitchens in the area, next up is a nursery

Erica: the Food Growers Initiative gave people a lot of hope during the hardlock down and gave a lot of people a purpose and meaning. And that's what's been human is all about, isn't it?

Busi “if I could I would stand on top of the hill and shout and say, guys, we can do it. We can just start.

Promo “A network of urban food gardens sprung up across Cape Town in response to the COVID 19 food crisis. Supported by their well off neighbours they were able to create havens of hope

Promo: The food crisis created by hard lockdown saw communities reaching out to each other and sparked a network of Urban food growers that will last far beyond the horror of 2020
